# Welcome {.unnumbered}

This is a lab guide to text mining in R. It is meant to give lab members a working sense of what the main text-mining techniques do, when each one is the right tool, and what each one cannot tell you.

We work through a single dataset the whole way. VCU CARES is a set of short interviews with VCU students about what the university does well, what worries them, and what they would change. Using one dataset means you can watch the same answers get described, grouped, scored, and predicted in different ways, and compare what each method gives you.

::: callout-important
## The data in this book are synthetic

The real VCU CARES responses are student statements and cannot be shared. The dataset used throughout this book is a **synthetic stand-in**: it has the same structure and size as the real workbook (three sheets, about 1,240 students, three questions each, and interviewer topic codes), but every word of text was generated. Nothing in it was said by a real student.

That makes it safe to publish and lets everyone run every line of code. It also means the *findings* are not findings. Differences between undergraduate and graduate students, for example, are random by construction. Use the book to learn the methods and to see how they behave, then apply them to real data.
:::

## The path through the book

The chapters move from methods that describe the text to methods that model it.

| Part | Chapter | What you learn |
|---|---|---|
| Getting started | 1. The data | Structure, cleaning, and what counts as a "document" |
| | 2. Tokens | Turning text into words, and counting them |
| Descriptive | 3. TF-IDF | Which words characterize one group of answers versus another |
| Finding structure | 4. Topic models I: LDA | Letting the computer propose themes |
| | 5. Topic models II: STM | Themes that can vary by student characteristics |
| | 6. Sentiment | Scoring how positive or negative the language is |
| Supervised learning | 7. Classification | Predicting the interviewers' topic codes from the text |
| | 8. Embeddings | Using a small pretrained language model, and how few labels you really need |
| | 9. Wrapping up | Choosing among methods, and reporting honestly |

Each chapter builds on the last, so I'd read them in order the first time.

## How to use this book

This book is written for people who are **not** already strong in statistics or programming. Each chapter explains the idea in plain language first, then shows the code, then walks through what each line does. If a term is unfamiliar, @sec-glossary defines it. If the R code looks unfamiliar, @sec-r-primer is a short guide to reading it.

You will see a few kinds of boxes in the margins of the text:

| Box | What it contains |
|---|---|
| **Note** (blue) | Extra background or a list of options worth knowing |
| **Tip** (green) | A habit or shortcut that will save you trouble |
| **Warning** (orange) | A common way to go wrong |
| **Important** (red) | Something that changes how you should read the results |


Each chapter follows the same shape. We state a question, run the code that answers it, and then read the output critically. Code appears in gray blocks, and you can copy any block by hovering over it and clicking the copy icon.

Work through a chapter with RStudio open next to your browser and run each block as you go. Text mining in particular rewards poking around: change a stop-word list, change the number of topics, and watch what moves.

::: callout-note
## Running it yourself

`SETUP.md` shows how to build the analysis file from the synthetic workbook in two commands. If you have approved access to the real VCU CARES workbook, you can point the same scripts at it. Real data must never be added to this repository; `.gitignore` keeps the `data/` folder out of version control.
:::

## Software you will need

You will need R and RStudio, both free, plus Quarto if you want to render the book yourself. Install the packages once:

```{r}
#| eval: false

install.packages(c(
  "tidyverse",    # data management and graphics
  "readxl",       # reading the Excel workbook
  "tidytext",     # tokenizing, TF-IDF, sentiment lexicons
  "topicmodels",  # LDA (Chapter 4)
  "stm",          # structural topic models (Chapter 5)
  "glmnet",       # regularized regression (Chapter 7)
  "ggraph",       # network plots of word pairs (Chapter 2)
  "igraph",       # used by ggraph
  "rsample",      # train/test splitting (Chapter 7)
  "reshape2",     # needed by tidytext to tidy topic models (Chapters 4-5)
  "ggrepel"       # non-overlapping chart labels (Chapter 8)
))
```

Chapter 8 also needs Python (and nothing else in the book does). `SETUP.md` has the short instructions. If you skip them, every other chapter still works.

`topicmodels` needs the GNU Scientific Library on some systems. If installation fails on Linux, install `libgsl-dev` first. Mac and Windows users usually have no problem.

## A word on what text mining is not

Text mining does not replace reading. Every method here compresses thousands of answers into something small enough to look at, and every compression loses something. Throughout the book I will ask you to go back to the original answers and check that the numbers mean what they seem to mean. That habit matters more than any particular function.
